title: Still open
hookLine: the questions this year didn't close
carry: a door you know the location of

lines: A DRAWER FOR WHAT DOESN'T FIT.
cards: Plenty of kitchens have one drawer for things that don't belong anywhere else: rubber bands, a key nobody can identify, the instructions for something you no longer own. You don't throw it out; you just know it's there.

A year of great questions has a drawer like that too. Suffering, death, love, work, forgiveness, awe: some got an answer you could hold. Some got a stack of answers that don't agree, or no answer at all.
Today the drawer opens, on purpose, and stays open.

teach.b: First, the question even the gods doubted. In the Katha Upanishad, a boy named Nachiketa, at the house of Death, asks what happens to a person after dying: some say he is, some say he is not.
Death answers that even the gods were once in doubt about this, that it's subtle and hard to know, and offers him wealth, long life and land if he'll ask anything else. Nachiketa keeps his question.
Some questions are worth more than every prize for dropping them.

teach.h: THE HYMN THAT WONDERS IF ANYONE KNOWS.
teach.b: Second, the hymn that wonders. The Hymn of Creation in the Rig Veda asks how everything began, and ends by wondering whether even the one who watches from the highest heaven knows, or perhaps does not know.
A sacred text that leaves its own question open.
Third, the brother who won't sign. In Dostoevsky's The Brothers Karamazov, Ivan says he can't accept a final harmony bought with a child's suffering.
His brother Alyosha, who believes, answers from his own faith but doesn't walk away, and the novel keeps them both at the table.
Fourth, open is not empty. These traditions have answers, and people live whole lives inside them. On this path, the answers stay in their own homes, and the choosing stays with you.
A question still open at the end of the year isn't a gap in the work. It's a door you know the location of.
Some people keep a list like this and look at it once a year, not to close the questions, but to see which changed shape, went quiet, or still wake them at night.

how: Some people on many paths keep a written list of their unanswered questions and return to it at the end of a year, noticing which ones have changed rather than trying to close them.

practice: Let the year's six questions pass by, suffering, death, love, work, forgiveness, awe, and notice which still tugs: a why, a what if, a person you can't make sense of. Write the open ones down plainly, one per line; three is plenty.
If you pray, bring the list into prayer; if not, keep it where you'll find it again.

wordCard.voice: Still open. The questions this year asked and didn't close: kept, named, and left on purpose with the door ajar. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: a door you know the location of. An open question can stay open. Back tomorrow, same hill.
